findings.title: Over-session failure names are keyed by product only, so names can be attributed to the wrong family
findings.description:
`over_sessions()` (`scripts/purchase_accounting.py:106`) filters coverage `volume_checks` on `verdict == "over"` and drops the `family` field that the coverage document actually provides (`volume_verdict_dict` in `src/manta_trading/data/tick/tick_coverage.py` emits `family` per volume check). `_family_evidence()` (`scripts/cutover_304_evidence.py`) accumulates those names into `named` keyed by product alone, and `over_failures()` then prints `named.get(row.product)` for *any* accounting row whose `traded_vs_cleared` over-count is non-zero. Two consequences:

- If more than one family of a product carries over counts (the tick tier is a volume family beside `bar_1m`; I could not fully confirm `VOLUME_FAMILIES`' membership from the files I read), each failure line lists every over session of the product, whichever family it belongs to, and the count in the line ("N sessions over") comes from a different instrument (the accounting row) than the names (the statistics coverage document), with no correspondence check between them.
- For a family whose coverage is never read — `coverage_reads()` covers only history wants, so the tick tier has no coverage doc — the failure line falls back to the `'?'` placeholder, naming nothing.

The exit rule still fails correctly (the count comes from accounting), but this script's product is an evidence report the PM reads; mis-attributed names in a failure line are a real defect of that report. Key `named` by `(product, family)` and include the `family` field in each name.

findings.title: `--estimate` reads cost figures without the unset guard, so a malformed payload escapes as a bare traceback
findings.description: `judge_estimate(..., check_ceilings=False)` returns `BUY` *before* the `_decimal(summary, "planned_usd")` validation (confirmed in `scripts/cutover_304_checks.py`), so in `--estimate` mode nothing checks the cost figures are present or numeric. `_estimate_only` then reads them raw: `planned = Decimal(summary["planned_usd"])` and `trailing = Decimal(summary["trailing_30d_usd"])`. `Decimal(None)` raises `TypeError` and a non-numeric string raises `decimal.InvalidOperation` — neither is a `KeyError`/`ValueError`, so `main`'s deliberate "unexpected payload" handler misses them. The operator gets an unnarrated traceback: nothing is written to the cutover log, which is the artifact the design says is the cutover's report. Reuse the existing `_decimal` guard (exposed from `cutover_304_checks`) or add `TypeError`/`InvalidOperation` to the payload handler so the stop is narrated. Note `final_failures` reads `planned_usd` the same raw way, but that is pre-existing code outside this diff's changes.

findings.title: `EXIT_USAGE` is defined but never used
findings.description: `EXIT_USAGE = 2` was added in this diff, but the argparse `SystemExit` handler in `main` uses `return int(exc.code or 0)` and nothing else references the constant. Remove it, or use it where the usage exit is produced.

findings.title: The "want has no end date" guard is implemented twice
findings.description: `latest_want_end()` (`scripts/purchase_verdicts.py`) and `coverage_reads()` (`scripts/cutover_304_evidence.py`) both walk `TICK_UNIVERSE` history and raise the identical "want has no end date" refusal for an open-ended want. Two copies of the same invariant over the same data can drift apart when one is edited. A single shared helper (the two modules already share `cutover_304_checks`) would keep one definition.

findings.title: Resubmit matching cannot distinguish the two products, which now share identical request keys
findings.description: `resubmit_origins` keys jobless requests by `(schema, range_start, range_end)`, and this diff's `_HISTORY_WANTS` gives ES and GC the *same* schema and range, so their requests collide on that key by construction (the docstring acknowledges this and takes the earliest, which errs toward refusal — the spend-safe direction). The residual risk is a false refusal with no in-script remedy: a resubmit of the product whose original was made after `since` is refused because the other product's earlier jobless request wins the `min()`. The debug rows carry `symbols`, so if the estimate's request rows ever expose per-request symbols, including them in `RequestKey` would remove the collision without weakening the guard. As written it is a documented, safe-direction tradeoff; recording it here so the limitation is visible in review.

structured_findings.summary: Over-session failure names are keyed by product only, so names can be attributed to the wrong family
`--estimate` reads cost figures without the unset guard, so a malformed payload escapes as a bare traceback
The "want has no end date" guard is implemented twice
Resubmit matching cannot distinguish the two products, which now share identical request keys
